omission_check: A separate word search flagged 173 words as "possibly missed" across 480 hospital records. It pointed at 1 of the full tool's 13 misses. 4 of those 13 are not real tool mistakes: 4 diagnosis names in our answer key have a double space, so the tool's correct answer was counted as missed (and as a false alarm). Most of the rest are combination medicines read as their two ingredients, which still look present by name, so the word search cannot spot them. It is a hint for the doctor, not a fact.

failure_examples.title: A premixed insulin is shown as two separate insulins
failure_examples.explanation: A held-out patient's Hospital B note said: "She is on insulin isophane and insulin regular twice a day." That is one premixed product, so the tool should have shown one insulin. It listed two separate insulins and no combined entry, so the product went missing. The wrong step was reading the note: the model took "and" to mean two medicines. This lost a combination product for 3 of 160 held-out patients. Names and quote still showed, so low harm. You can see the same mistake on sample patient P012.

failure_examples.title: A stopped medicine looks current again after the same split
failure_examples.explanation: Hospital A recorded paracetamol as stopped. A later Hospital B note said: "He takes paracetamol and hydrocodone when needed." The tool split that into a newer "paracetamol, current" entry, which overrode the stop; it should have shown paracetamol stopped. The stop is still visible in the history. This was one of the 2 planted "stopped at one hospital" tests the tool missed, because of the same split. A status came out wrong this way for 5 of 160 held-out patients. Low harm: paracetamol is in the combination anyway.

failure_examples.title: An opioid is listed twice, once alone and once in a combination
failure_examples.explanation: A held-out patient's Hospital B note said: "He takes paracetamol and oxycodone when needed." Hospitals A and C name the combination painkiller clearly, and the tool got that right. It also listed oxycodone as a separate current medicine, so the opioid appears twice; it should have shown only the combination. The wrong step was reading Hospital B's note. Extra entries like this appeared for 20 of 160 held-out patients. Low harm: nothing is missing and the quote is shown, but the list is longer and could prompt a needless question.
